summary: For ages 11–13: round numbers and measures to a stated number of decimal places or significant figures, and choose an accuracy appropriate to context. The central new skill is identifying significant figures (first sig fig = first non-zero digit; leading zeros never count; placeholder/trailing zeros do real work holding magnitude and recording precision), then making a single nearness/midpoint rounding decision and restoring place value with zeros (34,750 to 2 sf → 35,000, not 35).
misconceptions: Counting leading zeros as significant (0.0049 seen as 4 sig figs)
Dropping the placeholder zeros after rounding to sig figs (35,000 written as 35)
Confusing decimal places with significant figures
Truncating instead of rounding, or double-rounding through intermediate digits
Losing the trailing zero that records the rounded precision (2.90 written as 2.9 when 2 dp is required)

activities.title: Highlight the significant figures, round once, rebuild the size
steps: Take a number such as 34,750 and decide to round it to 2 significant figures.
Mark the counted significant digits (the 3 and the 4), confirming you start at the first non-zero digit.

Identify the single deciding digit immediately after the last required place (the 7) and place the number on a number line between its two candidate rounded values (34,000 and 35,000) and their midpoint (34,500); decide the round-up in one step.
Reassemble the answer as 35,000, writing in the placeholder zeros that keep the number in the thousands — do NOT stop at 35.

Now take 0.004982 and round to 2 significant figures: cross out the leading zeros as 'not significant', count the 4 and 9, apply the deciding digit (8) so 49 rounds up to 50, and write 0.0050 — keeping the front zeros for magnitude and the trailing zero for precision.
Repeat 0.004982 rounded to 2 decimal places (= 0.00) and place both answers side by side to see that dp and sf give genuinely different results.
activities.insight: Significant figures are counted from the first non-zero digit; zeros can be placeholders that hold a number's size or trailing zeros that record precision, so they cannot simply be dropped. Rounding is one nearness decision based on the next digit, after which place value must be restored.

activities.title: Contrast decimal places with significant figures on one number
steps: Pick a single number (e.g. 0.004982) and round it both to 2 decimal places and to 2 significant figures.
Record the two answers side by side (0.00 vs 0.0050) and write a sentence explaining why they differ.
Do the same for a large number such as 47,320: to 2 sf it is 47,000 (zeros needed), and note how that differs from a decimal-place instruction.
State in your own words when leading zeros are ignored and when zeros must be kept.
activities.insight: Decimal places and significant figures are different rules: dp counts from the decimal point, while sf counts from the first non-zero digit. The difference is most striking with leading zeros and with large numbers that need placeholder zeros, but they also differ for ordinary numbers (3.14159 is 3.14 to 2 dp and 3.1 to 2 sf). The same number can give very different rounded values under each.

activities.title: Choose and justify an appropriate degree of accuracy
steps: Given a context such as measuring a room's length, decide whether rounding to 2 decimal places or 2 significant figures is more appropriate, and explain why.
Explain to a partner (or in writing) why 47,320 to 2 sf needs its zeros on the end but 47 to 2 sf would not.
Respond to a challenge like: 'You rounded 34,750 to 2 significant figures and wrote 35 — convince me that is the right size.'
Justify which single digit decided each of your roundings and why the remaining digits did not matter.
activities.insight: Accuracy should suit the precision of the measurement or context, and learners should be able to justify both the rounded value's size and the choice of dp vs sf.

activities.title: Consolidation: quick-check rounding problems
steps: Round 0.004982 to 2 significant figures, choosing from answers that include the dp-confusion value 0.00 so you can check you avoid it (the correct value is 0.0050).
Round 2.988 to 2 dp (→ 2.99, a simple round-up) and 1.998 to 2 dp (→ 2.00, where the round-up carries through several places and the trailing zeros must be written).
activities.insight: After building the identification skill, learners can reliably apply dp and sf rounding, including the round-up cascade and placeholder/trailing zeros, in short targeted items.

checkQuestion: Round these, showing your steps. (1) 3.14159 to 2 decimal places. (2) 0.004621 to 2 significant figures. (3) 47,320 to 2 significant figures.
